summary:
Morelos is a state within Mexico, and the rules a trans visitor would face there stand under the national framework rather than under any Morelos-specific statute: the sources vetted for this record carry no Morelos enactment, enforcement incident or lethality figure. Legal gender recognition in Mexico is legislated state by state.

Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, that two more states operate one in practice without enactment, that six legislatures have enacted nothing, and that only seven states extend recognition to children. The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation has set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure.

Where no procedure exists, Human Rights Watch records identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents documented in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion reported on 6 March 2024 on the state of Tabasco, which lacks a legal gender-recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance under scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are shut out of employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The report sets those barriers against the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and against the finding that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.
tangentialFactors:
Tabasco and Guanajuato are the documented reference points for the obstructed end of the national spectrum. In Tabasco, as of March 2024, the absence of a procedure was translating into blocked access to employment, health services, education and financial transactions; in Guanajuato, Human Rights Watch recorded incidents arising from identity-document mismatch.

The surrounding violence risk is measured nationally rather than locally: more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, and the Tabasco file records the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa.

The national picture is uneven in both directions. Two states run a recognition procedure in practice without having enacted one, while six legislatures have enacted nothing at all, so formal statute and lived administrative practice do not line up across the country.

Recognition for children is a narrow exception: only seven of the 32 states extend it, which bears on families travelling with a trans minor even where adult recognition is available.
localsOnly:
Morelos residents apply for identity documents under the national framework of Mexico, in which the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation's guidelines bind the states and, since 2022, extend legal gender recognition to minors. Only seven of Mexico's 32 states extend recognition to children through their own procedures.

Residents' access depends as much on administrative practice as on statute. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that two states run a recognition procedure in practice without legislative enactment, while six legislatures have enacted nothing.

The consequences recorded for residents without matching documents are administrative and daily: discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, and where a procedure is absent, exclusion from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. Each document request or appearance under scrutiny carries a risk of harassment and humiliation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The vetted sources carry no Morelos-specific statute, administrative procedure, enforcement incident or lethality figure. Whether Morelos is among the 22 states with a legislated recognition procedure, the two operating one in practice, or the six with none, is unresolved for this record.

Whether Morelos extends legal gender recognition to children is not sourced here either; the national count of seven states is not broken down by state in the material available.

The 2022 impunity figure for homicides and the killing of Karina Gomez in Villahermosa are, respectively, a national statistic and a Tabasco-specific incident. Their bearing on Morelos is not established by the sources.

Human Rights Watch's 31 March 2025 account of identity-document mismatch in Guanajuato and Tabasco gives no state-by-state list of documented incidents, so Morelos cannot be placed on or off that list from this material.
